Series::zeta¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::zeta(double other) const

What It Does¶

Computes the Hurwitz zeta function elementwise. self supplies the exponent x; the argument supplies the offset q:

zeta(x, q) = sum_{k>=0} (q + k)^(-x)

With q = 1 this is the Riemann zeta function, zeta(x) = sum_{n>=1} n^(-x). The Hurwitz form generalizes the sum to start from q instead of 1, and it is the piece the polygamma functions are built from:

polygamma(n, q) = (-1)^(n+1) * n! * zeta(n + 1, q)      for n >= 1

So polygamma — and therefore the gradient of digamma — routes through this function.

The forward pass uses Euler-Maclaurin acceleration: a short direct sum takes the offset past ~9, then an asymptotic correction with Bernoulli coefficients converges to full float64 precision in a handful of terms.

Domain:

  • x = 1 is the harmonic pole; zeta(1, q) returns +inf.

  • x < 1 returns NaN; this method does not provide analytic continuation in the exponent.

  • Positive q is the ordinary Hurwitz-zeta domain.

  • A non-positive integer q places one term of the series on a pole and returns +inf.

  • A negative, non-integral q is supported when x is an integer. For a non-integral exponent, raising the negative leading terms to -x would leave the real number system, so the real-valued method returns NaN.

Parameters¶

other (double): the offset q, a scalar constant applied to every element of self.

Returns¶

Series A Series with the same shape as self, each element zeta(x, q), or +inf / NaN on the domain boundary.

An integral input is promoted to float64.

Gradient¶

The method form is not differentiable. self is the exponent x, whose derivative — sum_k -ln(q + k) (q + k)^(-x) — has no routing here and matches the not_implemented status the exponent slot has elsewhere. q arrives as a plain double, so it is a constant.

An objective that reaches its input only through zeta is therefore disconnected: if self tracks slope, calling reverse() on it raises (Example 5). The offset derivative that does have a closed form, d/dq zeta(x, q) = -x * zeta(x + 1, q), applies only when q is supplied as a differentiable series through the lower-level routing layer, not through this method.

Examples¶

Example 1. With q = 1 this is the Riemann zeta. zeta(2) = pi^2/6, zeta(4) = pi^4/90, zeta(6) = pi^6/945.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({2.0, 4.0, 6.0}).zeta(1.0)
) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1.6449, 1.0823, 1.0173]

Example 2. The Hurwitz offset. zeta(2, 1), zeta(2, 2), zeta(2, 3) each drop the leading terms of the Riemann sum.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({2.0, 2.0, 2.0}).zeta(1.0)
) << "\n";
pluss::series::print(std::cout, pluss::make_series({2.0}).zeta(2.0)) << "\n";
pluss::series::print(std::cout, pluss::make_series({2.0}).zeta(3.0)) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1.6449, 1.6449, 1.6449]
Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[0.6449]
Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[0.3949]

zeta(2, 2) = zeta(2) - 1 = 0.6449341, and zeta(2, 3) = zeta(2) - 1 - 1/4 = 0.3949341.

Example 3. The recurrence zeta(x, q) - zeta(x, q + 1) = q^(-x).

auto exponents = pluss::make_series({2.0, 3.0});
auto dropped_term = exponents.zeta(1.0).sub(exponents.zeta(2.0));
pluss::series::print(std::cout, dropped_term) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[1.0000, 1.0000]

Here q = 1, so the removed leading term is 1^(-x) = 1 for both exponents. This recurrence is useful when shifting an awkward offset into a more convenient range.

Example 4. A negative fractional offset distinguishes three cases. Integral exponents remain real, a fractional exponent does not, and a non-positive integer offset is a pole.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({2.0, 3.0, 2.5}).zeta(-0.5)
) << "\n";
pluss::series::print(std::cout, pluss::make_series({2.0}).zeta(0.0)) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[8.9348, 0.4144, nan]
Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[inf]

Example 5. The method form is non-differentiable. Tracking the exponent does not make the result track slope because this public overload has no exponent backward rule.

auto s = pluss::make_series({2.0, 3.0});
s.tracks_slope_(true);
auto obj = s.zeta(1.0).sum();
std::cout << "exponent tracks: " << s.tracks_slope() << "\n";
std::cout << "objective tracks: " << obj.tracks_slope() << "\n";

Output¶

exponent tracks: 1
objective tracks: 0

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • Argument order: self is the exponent x, the argument is the offset q. x.zeta(1.0) is the ordinary Riemann zeta of x.

  • x must be strictly greater than 1. x = 1 returns +inf; x < 1 returns NaN. This routine does not do analytic continuation into the critical strip.

  • Negative fractional q is real only for integral x. A non-positive integer q is a pole and returns +inf.

  • The method form carries no gradient. Do not place a tracked series in the exponent and expect a sensitivity — reverse() will raise.

Summary¶

zeta(q) is the Hurwitz zeta sum_{k>=0} (q + k)^(-x), with the exponent x from self and the offset q from the argument:

  • zeta(1.0) is the Riemann zeta; zeta(2) = pi^2/6

  • the closed form behind polygamma for n >= 1

  • requires x > 1; positive q is the ordinary domain, while negative q follows the real-valued integral-exponent rules described above

  • the method form is non-differentiable

See Also¶

  • Series::polygamma: built from zeta(n + 1, x).

  • Series::digamma: its gradient routes through this function.

  • Series::lgamma: the other core gamma-family special function.
